citations.quote:
An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

If $X\in\mathbb R^p$ is measurable and $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$, then
$\mu=\mathbb E X$ and $\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T]$ in
[[def-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]] are well-defined entrywise,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

Let $n,p\ge1$ be integers and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent identically distributed random vectors in $\mathbb R^p$ with finite second moments, mean $\mu=\mathbb E X_1$, and covariance matrix
$$\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X_1-\mu)(X_1-\mu)^{\mathsf T}].$$
The oracle-centered sample covariance and the sample-centered covariance are respectively
$$\widehat\Sigma_\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(X_i-\mu)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat\Sigma^\ast=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T},\quad \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
For a matrix estimate $A$, squared operator loss is $\|A-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, with the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. This definition distinguishes the known-mean raw second moment from the estimator that removes an unknown mean.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

derivations.claim: Regard $\mathbb S^p$ as the subspace of $\mathbb R^{p^2}$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Each matrix coordinate of $T_n$ is a polynomial in the $np$ real sample coordinates, so $T_n:(\mathbb R^p)^n\to\mathbb R^{p^2}$ is continuous. Its values are symmetric because every outer product is symmetric, hence it is also continuous as a map into the subspace $\mathbb S^p$. By [F7] it is Borel measurable.

By [F1] and [F2], the sample experiment is the stated parameter-indexed iid experiment; [F3] places $\Sigma_\theta$ in $\mathbb S^p$, and [F4] identifies it as the estimand target. The formula in [F5] is exactly $T_n$. Thus [F6] and step 1.1 make $T_n$ a statistic and, since its target space is the same $\mathbb S^p$, an estimator of $\psi$.
